jdso8u-d1e1293-d1e105.summary: Editorial title of the single question for distinction 37 (Wadding edition), framing it as whether God's presence everywhere by power implies his presence everywhere by essence, i.e. whether omnipotence entails immensity.

jdso8u-d1e1293-d1e121.summary: Editorial apparatus of parallel loci: a list of where earlier and later scholastics (Alexander of Hales, Henry of Ghent, Aquinas, Bonaventure, Richard of Middleton, Durand, Capreolus, Biel, Suárez, Vázquez, Ockham, Bassolis, Mair) and Scotus himself treat the same question. It locates the question within a long debate rather than advancing an argument.

jdso8u-d1e1293-d1e147.summary: Scotus states the question and gives the principal argument for the affirmative: since, following Aristotle's Physics VII, every agent must be present to what it acts on (immediately if it acts immediately), and an omnipotent agent can act immediately on anything, God must be immediately present to everything. Omnipotence would thus entail essential omnipresence.
claims: Every agent is present to its patient, immediately if it acts immediately (Aristotle, Physics VII).
An omnipotent agent can act immediately on anything.
Therefore the omnipotent agent is immediately present to everything.

jdso8u-d1e1293-d1e187.summary: The argument for the opposite: God can cause something outside the universe where he is not now present by essence, so his power to act somewhere does not presuppose his essential presence there.
claims: God can cause something beyond the universe.
God is not now present by essence beyond the universe.
Hence power to act at a place does not require essential presence there.

jdso8u-d1e1293-d1e202.summary: Heading marking the start of the editor's scholium, an editorial aid distinct from Scotus's text.

jdso8u-d1e1293-d1e207.summary: The editor's scholium summarizes Scotus's position: God is indeed everywhere, but this does not follow from his operation as Aquinas holds. It lists Scotus's three reasons (acting only on what is co-present is an imperfection of created causes; God's power is his will, which can will what is distant; God created the world where he was not before), names followers (Ockham, Biel, Bassolis, the Scotists), and defends Scotus against critics who cite Acts 17, reading that text as about the ease of knowing God rather than about immensity.
claims: Scotus holds that God is everywhere but that this cannot be proved from divine operation.
Acts 17:27-28 concerns knowledge of God, not divine immensity, and so does not tell against Scotus.

jdso8u-d1e1293-d1e249.summary: Scotus's reply begins by examining created agents. A created agent can act where it is not, though it normally must be next to the nearest patient. Even then it may not act on the near patient with the same kind of action it exerts on the distant one (the torpedo fish numbs the fisherman's hand but not the net), or it may act on the near patient by a different active power (a heavenly body generates minerals deep in the earth by its substantial form while affecting the intervening medium differently). Where such contact is needed, it comes either from the joining of two active powers in one agent, each proportioned to a different patient, or from the agent's imperfection, which forces it to produce the less perfect effect first.
claims: A created agent can act on a distant patient where it is not.
An agent may act on a distant patient without acting on the intermediate one with the same power.
The need to act on the proximate patient first comes either from two active powers combined in one agent or from imperfection in the agent's active power.
concepts: substantial form as principle of action

jdso8u-d1e1293-d1e351.summary: Applying the analysis: remove from an agent both the concurrence of two powers and the imperfection that makes it produce the less perfect first, and nothing stops it from being present by power to a distant patient without acting on the near one. The more perfect a form, the more remote its reach. Omnipotence is a simply perfect active power that needs neither condition, so it is a principle of producing anything possible even if, per impossibile, its bearer were not everywhere.
claims: Without concurrent powers or imperfection, an agent need not act on the proximate patient in order to act on the remote one.
The more perfect an active form, the more it is a principle of acting at a distance.
Omnipotence, as simply perfect active power, could produce anything possible even if its subject were not everywhere.

jdso8u-d1e1293-d1e423.summary: Scotus concludes that the negative answer should be held: omnipotence does not entail immensity. He confirms it from the will: omnipotence is a will whose willing is followed by the thing's existing; a will can will something distant as easily as something near; so an omnipotent being confined, per impossibile, to one place could still make something exist elsewhere without being there by essence.
claims: Omnipotence does not entail immensity.
Divine omnipotence is the will whose volition is followed by the existence of the thing willed.
A will can will the distant as readily as the near.
An omnipotent being located in one place could still cause effects elsewhere by willing them.

jdso8u-d1e1293-d1e461.summary: A second confirmation from creation: before the world there was no infinite empty space in which God was essentially present, yet God was able to make the world. So at creation presence by power came first and did not presuppose presence by essence; the power had its term before there was any essential presence. Likewise now God need not be conceived as first present in some part of the universe in order to cause there; rather he is there first by power, and could cause there even if, per impossibile, he were not first there by essence.
claims: Before creation there was no imaginary infinite void where God was present by essence.
God's power to create did not presuppose essential presence where the world was made.
Presence by power is prior to, and does not depend on, presence by essence.

jdso8u-d1e1293-d1e513.summary: Reply to the initial argument: Aristotle's principle that the agent must be present to the patient holds for natural agents acting by natural qualities or forms, which act on the distant only through concurrent forms that act on the near. It does not hold for the will, by which the omnipotent acts.
claims: The principle that agent and patient must be together applies only to natural agents acting by natural forms.
It does not apply to the will, through which God acts.

jdso8u-d1e1293-Dd1e102.summary: Opening section of the question: an editorial title and list of parallel loci, then Scotus's statement of the question (does presence everywhere by power imply presence everywhere by essence?), the Aristotelian argument that an omnipotent agent must be immediately present to everything it can act on, and the counter-argument that God can cause beyond the universe where he is not by essence.
claims: The affirmative rests on the Aristotelian principle that agent and patient must be together.
The negative rests on God's ability to cause beyond the universe.

jdso8u-d1e1293-Dd1e199.summary: Scotus's resolution, preceded by the editor's scholium. He analyses how created agents act at a distance and traces their need for contact with the proximate patient to either concurrent powers or imperfection. Since omnipotence is a simply perfect power with neither feature, it can act anywhere without presupposing essential presence. He takes the negative side and confirms it twice: omnipotence is a will, which can will the distant as easily as the near; and at creation God's power reached its term without prior essential presence in any void. The Aristotelian principle of agent-patient contact is restricted to natural agents.
claims: Omnipotence does not entail immensity; God's presence everywhere cannot be deduced from his power to act everywhere.
The need for contact between agent and patient comes from concurrent powers or imperfection, which omnipotence lacks.
God acts by will, which is not bound by distance.
Presence by power is prior to presence by essence, as creation shows.
The Aristotelian contact principle holds only for natural agents.

jdso8u-d1e1293.summary: Ordinatio I d.37, single question (Wadding edition, with editorial title, parallel loci and scholium): whether God's omnipotence entails his immensity, i.e. whether presence everywhere by power implies presence everywhere by essence. Against the Aristotelian argument that an agent must be present to what it acts on, Scotus argues that this requirement comes from features of imperfect created agents (concurrent powers, imperfection of active power) that a simply perfect power lacks. Since omnipotence is a will that can will the distant as readily as the near, and since at creation God's power did not presuppose his essential presence anywhere, Scotus holds the negative: omnipotence does not imply immensity. God is in fact everywhere, but this cannot be proved from his causal activity, and the contact principle is confined to natural agents.
claims: Divine omnipotence does not logically entail divine immensity.
Presence by power is prior to and independent of presence by essence.
God acts by will, so the natural requirement of agent-patient contact does not bind him.
Demonstrating divine omnipresence from divine operation (as in Aquinas) fails.
